verses.text: Some time later God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" "Here I am," he answered.
"Take your son," God said, "your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you."

So Abraham got up early the next morning, saddled his donkey, and took along two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for a burnt offering and set out for the place God had designated.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance.
"Stay here with the donkey," Abraham told his servants. "The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you."
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife, and the two of them walked on together.
Then Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" "Here I am, my son," he replied. "The fire and the wood are here," said Isaac, "but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?"
Abraham answered, "God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son." And the two walked on together.
When they arrived at the place God had designated, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood.
Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven, "Abraham, Abraham!" "Here I am," he replied.
"Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him," said the angel, "for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me."
Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.
And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. So to this day it is said, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided."
And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time,
saying, "By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son,
I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies.
And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice."
Abraham went back to his servants, and they got up and set out together for Beersheba. And Abraham settled in Beersheba.
Some time later, Abraham was told, "Milcah has also borne sons to your brother Nahor:
Uz the firstborn, his brother Buz, Kemuel (the father of Aram),
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."
And Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham's brother Nahor.
Moreover, Nahor's concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Abraham, Sarah and their family (Genesis 11:27 to 25:11)
context.audience: Israel, the children of Abraham, learning how God’s promise began
context.setting: “Some time later God tested Abraham” (v.1). “Take your son,” God says, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering” (v.2). Early in the morning Abraham saddles his donkey, cuts the wood and sets out (v.3). On the third day he sees the place and tells his servants, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you” (v.5). Isaac carries the wood; Abraham carries the fire and the knife (v.6). “Where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” Isaac asks, and Abraham answers, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (vv.7-8). Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac and lays him on the wood, and takes the knife, but the angel of the LORD calls: “Do not lay a hand on the boy” (vv.9-12). Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and offers it “in place of his son” (v.13). He names the place “The LORD Will Provide” (v.14). God swears by Himself to bless him and multiply his descendants “like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore,” and “through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed” (vv.16-18). The chapter ends with news of his brother Nahor’s family, including Rebekah (vv.20-24).
context.custom: Child sacrifice was practiced by some peoples of Canaan and its neighbors, especially in times of crisis (2 Kings 3:27). The law of Moses forbids it as detestable (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). The story ends with God stopping the knife and providing a substitute; later, every firstborn son in Israel was to be redeemed, not sacrificed (Exodus 13:13). Jewish tradition calls this chapter the Akedah, ‘the binding,’ and reads it at the New Year.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 23 tells of Sarah’s death and how Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron to bury her.
context.timelineBible: Hebrews says Abraham “reasoned that God could raise the dead” (Hebrews 11:19), and James calls the offering of Isaac faith shown in action (James 2:21-23). Christians have long seen the story as a picture of the Father who “did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32); Jesus carried His own cross as Isaac carried the wood, and John the Baptist called Him “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29). Second Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple “on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3:1).

translation.meaning: To test, try, prove. The narrator tells the reader at the start that this is a test.
Hinneni, ‘here I am’: the answer of a servant ready to act. Abraham says it three times: to God (v.1), to Isaac (v.7) and to the angel (v.11).
Only, unique, beloved. Ishmael was also Abraham’s son, but Isaac was the one son of the promise. The Greek Old Testament translates ‘beloved.’
To see. ‘God will see to it’: Yahweh-yireh, ‘the LORD will see’ or ‘provide.’

gospelParallels.note: Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead.

Faith was made complete by what he did.

overview.summary: God tests Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac as a burnt offering; Abraham obeys, saying God will provide the lamb, and at the last moment the angel stops him and God provides a ram in Isaac’s place; God swears to bless all nations through his offspring.
overview.settingLine: A mountain in the land of Moriah.
overview.placeName: The land of Moriah (Jerusalem by tradition)

history.t: Practiced by neighbors; forbidden in Israel.

customs.t: Time to turn back, and he does not.

archaeology.t: A Phoenician burial ground of infant urns, often linked with child sacrifice, though this is debated.
The rock under the Dome of the Rock is traditionally the place of the binding.

overview.discussion: Abraham told Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb” (v.8). What am I holding so tightly that I would struggle to trust God with it?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters (1-25 in the app so far). Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham and his family.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

historicalImage.caption: The Sacrifice of Isaac, attributed to Caravaggio (about 1598; the attribution of this version is debated). The angel stops Abraham as the knife is drawn, and the ram waits at the lower left: “Do not lay a hand on the boy” (Genesis 22:12).

currentImage.caption: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem with the Dome of the Rock. Solomon built the temple “on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3:1), and Jewish tradition connects it with the mountain in “the land of Moriah” where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2).
